title: Casper and the Bakery
premise: Wendell Montrose built a career orchestrating other people's perfect days after his own life collapsed a decade ago, hiding behind flawless events and unanswered letters he never sent. When Casper Reyes—the baker who wrote to him every month for ten years under a pen name, letters Wendell answered in kind without ever learning the truth—moves into the apartment next door, the anonymity that protected them both begins to unravel. As the town's harvest festival approaches, Wendell must plan one last wedding while confronting what those letters really cost him: the identity he invented to survive. In the end, Wendell walks away from the biggest contract of his career, admits he knew who Casper was all along, and chooses an unwritten future over the safe, invisible one.
about_author: Lena Joubert is the pen name of a former event coordinator who spent six years watching love from behind catering tables before turning to fiction. She writes about people who are better at arranging happiness than claiming it, and lives above a bakery she refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Last Contract
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He signs the festival-season wedding of the year—a society bride with an unlimited budget—while privately drafting his resignation letter for the hundredth time. The emotional beat is weary competence masking quiet despair; he plans joy he no longer believes in.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, flashback-tinged. We learn of the decade-long correspondence with 'C.'—monthly letters exchanged through a bookstore's anonymous post box—and why Wendell stopped answering two years ago. The beat is tender regret; memory as both shelter and wound.

chapters.title: Flour on the Landing
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A moving truck arrives next door; the new tenant leaves a welcome basket of sourdough on his step with a note in handwriting Wendell recognizes instantly. He doesn't knock. The beat is panic disguised as politeness.

chapters.title: Casper
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Introduce him properly: a baker who closed his failing city shop to start over, carrying a shoebox of returned letters he never had the courage to sign. He recognizes Wendell too. The beat is hopeful dread—he came here on purpose.

chapters.title: Small Talk, Large Silences
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Stairwell encounters grow longer; both perform casualness while testing each other with loaded small talk about bread, weather, and 'people who disappear.' The beat is mutual suspicion wrapped in warmth.

chapters.title: The Bride Who Wants Everything
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The festival wedding escalates into a monster: three venues, a live orchestra, a bride who wants 'authenticity' staged perfectly. Wendell's assistant notices he's distracted. The beat is mounting pressure; survival demanding more of him than ever.

chapters.title: Tasting Menu
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The bride insists on a local baker; Wendell is forced to hire Casper for the wedding cake. Their first real collaboration crackles with things unsaid. The beat is dangerous intimacy—working together means being seen.

chapters.title: What the Letters Said
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Alone at night, Casper rereads the correspondence and realizes Wendell's replies stopped right after the letter where 'C.' almost revealed his name. The beat is grief sharpening into resolve: he will make Wendell say it out loud.

chapters.title: Festival Preparations
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The town gears up for the harvest festival; lanterns, stalls, a dance floor in the square. Casper's pop-up bakery becomes the heart of it, and Wendell can't avoid the crowd—or him. The beat is community warmth tightening the trap of proximity.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A late night in the nearly-finished festival square; wine, honest laughter, a moment that almost becomes a kiss—until Wendell retreats with a lie about deadlines. The beat is self-sabotage; the price of survival paid in loneliness.

chapters.title: The Assistant's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. His assistant Priya confronts him: she found the old letters in his desk, she knows who Casper is, and she tells him the wedding will destroy them both if he keeps pretending. The beat is confrontation; truth spoken by proxy.

chapters.title: Burnt Sugar
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. A cake-tasting disaster—Casper burns a batch after seeing Wendell with his ex-business partner—and an argument spills into the alley. Casper accuses him of running; Wendell says 'you don't know what I gave up.' The beat is rupture.

chapters.title: Ten Years Ago
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, full flashback. The collapse: the failed business, the family shame, how a stranger's first anonymous letter pulled him back from the edge—and how answering it became the only honest thing in his life. The beat is devastating context; survival has a price tag.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal Dinner
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wendell flawlessly executes the rehearsal dinner while falling apart inside; Casper caters it and watches him perform. They share one quiet moment over dirty dishes where neither pretends anymore—but neither speaks either. The beat is exhausted honesty without resolution.

chapters.title: Priya's Discovery
chapters.summary: Priya's POV (brief). She realizes Wendell has been quietly funneling his own savings into covering the bride's cost overruns to keep the wedding alive—an act of penance, not ambition. The beat is revelation; Wendell's 'career that saved everything' is bleeding him dry.

chapters.title: The Letter He Kept
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper finds the one letter Wendell never mailed—slipped under his door years ago by mistake, kept all this time—in which Wendell admitted he'd figured out who C. was. The beat is heartbreak inverted: Wendell always knew, and stayed silent to protect them both.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Cold Room
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The night before the wedding, Casper corners Wendell among the refrigerated flowers. Everything comes out: the letters, the silence, the near-missed decade. Wendell finally says his name aloud. The beat is cathartic collision—climax of feeling, not yet of plot.

chapters.title: The Wedding Day
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The festival wedding unfolds in perfection—and Wendell watches the bride marry a man she barely knows because it's practical, a mirror of his own bargains. Mid-ceremony, he makes his decision. The beat is clarity arriving at the worst possible moment.

chapters.title: Walking Out
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He hands Priya the emergency binder, tells the bride the truth about the budget, and walks out mid-reception past the lanterns and the band. The beat is terrifying liberation; the career that saved him released at last.

chapters.title: Where the Festival Ends
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper, certain he's lost him again, is closing his stall when Wendell appears in the emptying square holding the unmailed letter and the shoebox of replies. No speeches—just the truth, finally signed. The beat is quiet climax; recognition at last.

chapters.title: First Morning
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The morning after: flour on the landing again, but this time they bake together before dawn, trading the letters' private jokes out loud for the first time. The beat is tentative joy; identity rebuilt rather than hidden.

chapters.title: Caspar and the Bakery
chapters.summary: Epilogue, both POVs. Months later: a small storefront with both their names, no grand weddings planned, just a town that shows up for bread. Wendell writes one final letter—to himself—and mails it. The beat is earned peace; second chances were always about timing, and theirs arrived.
